# Overview

TweedSpot detects spatially variable genes (SVGs) in spatial transcriptomics
data using Tweedie generalized additive models (GAMs) with a spatial smooth.
The package currently focuses on an agnostic SVG workflow built around the
`SpatialExperiment` container.

TweedSpot is intended to be useful to the broader spatial transcriptomics
community, especially for analysts who want a method that models count data
directly, adapts to heterogeneous mean-variance relationships, and plugs into
standard downstream workflows for ranking, visualization, and interpretation of
spatially variable genes. We are submitting the package to Bioconductor
because we think it can serve as a broadly accessible, reproducible tool for
community use and comparison across spatial datasets and analysis pipelines.

Once available on Bioconductor, the release version can be installed with:

```{r eval = FALSE}
install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("TweedSpot")
```

The current development version can be installed from GitHub with:

```{r eval = FALSE}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("himelmallick/TweedSpot", dependencies = TRUE)
```

This vignette covers a standard workflow:

1. load a `SpatialExperiment`
2. prefilter low-information genes
3. fit TweedSpot
4. extract and rank gene-level results
5. visualize observed and fitted spatial patterns

# Load packages

```{r libraries}
library(TweedSpot)
library(SpatialExperiment)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
library(STexampleData)
library(BiocParallel)
```

# Load example data

We use the `Visium_humanDLPFC()` example dataset from `STexampleData`. To keep
the vignette lightweight, we restrict the analysis to in-tissue spots and a
small subset of genes.

```{r load-data}
spe <- Visium_humanDLPFC()
spe <- spe[, colData(spe)$in_tissue == 1]
spe <- spe[seq_len(min(250, nrow(spe))), ]
spe
```

# Prefilter features

`filter_features()` removes features with limited information before model
fitting. Its thresholds (minimum total signal, percent and number of locations
where the feature is detected, mean, and variance) make no assumption about the
assay, so the same call works for genes, proteins, peaks, or metabolites. For
intensity data, `detection_threshold` sets the value above which a feature
counts as detected. Named features such as negative-control probes can be
removed with `exclude` or `exclude_pattern`, and, for transcriptomics only,
`exclude_mito` and `exclude_ribo` remove mitochondrial and ribosomal genes.

Two further steps are specific to TweedSpot. First, by default
(`model_aware = TRUE`) a feature must be detected in at least as many
locations as the spatial smooth has basis functions, so pass the same
`smooth_k` you will use in `tweedspot()`. Second, locations can be quality
controlled with `min_total_per_location`, `min_features_per_location`,
`outlier_nmads`, `max_excluded_fraction` (for example the mitochondrial
fraction), and `location_mask`. Use `action = "flag"` to keep everything and
record the reasons in `filter_keep` and `filter_reason` columns instead.

```{r filter-features}
spe <- TweedSpot::filter_features(
  input = spe,
  assay_name = "counts",
  min_total = 5,
  min_pct_locations = 5,
  min_locations = 3,
  min_mean = 0.05,
  drop_empty_locations = TRUE,
  report = TRUE
)

spe
```

# Fit TweedSpot

We now fit TweedSpot on the filtered dataset. For this example object,
`sample_id` is constant across all retained spots, so we do not include it as a
covariate. To keep the vignette fast and robust across build machines, this
runnable example uses the Poisson mapping (`tweedie_p = 1`), total-count
library-size offsets, serial execution, and a small `smooth_k`. Estimated
Tweedie fits with `tweedie_p = NULL` and SCRAN size factors are shown below as
recommended analysis options for full datasets.

```{r run-tweedspot}


bp <- SerialParam()

spe_res <- tweedspot(
  input = spe,
  assay_name = "counts",
  two_part = FALSE,
  tweedie_p = 1,
  fit_method = "REML",
  use_bam = FALSE,
  bam_discrete = TRUE,
  size_factor_method = "library_size",
  smooth_k = 5,
  BPPARAM = bp,
  verbose = TRUE
)
```

# Tweedie index parameter

TweedSpot is built on `mgcv`, so its Tweedie index support follows what can be
represented as `mgcv` families. The main control is `tweedie_p`.

When `tweedie_p = NULL`, TweedSpot uses `mgcv::tw()` and estimates the Tweedie
index during fitting. This is the default and recommended setting for raw
spatial transcriptomics count data because genes can differ substantially in
their mean-variance relationships.

Fixed values are also supported:

| `tweedie_p` | Family used internally | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `NULL` | `mgcv::tw()` | Estimated Tweedie index |
| `0` | `stats::gaussian()` | Gaussian model for continuous approximately normal outcomes |
| `1` | `stats::poisson()` | Poisson count model |
| `1 < p < 2` | `mgcv::Tweedie(p = p)` | Compound Poisson-Gamma Tweedie model |
| `2` | `mgcv::Tweedie(p = 2)` | Gamma boundary case |
| `3` | `stats::inverse.gaussian()` | Inverse Gaussian model for strictly positive outcomes |

Values between `0` and `1`, values between `2` and `3`, negative values, and
values greater than `3` are not supported. The inverse Gaussian case requires
strictly positive responses, so it should not be used on raw count assays that
contain zeros.

For example, users can fit a fixed Tweedie index:

```{r fixed-tweedie-p, eval = FALSE}
spe_res_fixed <- tweedspot(
  input = spe,
  assay_name = "counts",
  tweedie_p = 1.5,
  use_bam = TRUE,
  bam_discrete = TRUE,
  smooth_k = 10
)
```

Or use the Poisson and Gaussian mappings when those assumptions are desired:

```{r alternate-index-settings, eval = FALSE}
spe_res_poisson <- tweedspot(
  input = spe,
  assay_name = "counts",
  tweedie_p = 1
)

spe_res_gaussian <- tweedspot(
  input = spe,
  assay_name = "counts",
  tweedie_p = 0
)
```

The `family` argument remains available for users who want to pass an `mgcv`
family directly, but `tweedie_p` takes precedence when both are supplied.

For a full analysis, users may prefer the adaptive Tweedie model with SCRAN size
factors:

```{r adaptive-tweedie-scran, eval = FALSE}
spe_res <- tweedspot(
  input = spe,
  assay_name = "counts",
  tweedie_p = NULL,
  use_bam = TRUE,
  bam_discrete = TRUE,
  size_factor_method = "scran",
  smooth_k = 10,
  BPPARAM = BiocParallel::bpparam()
)
```

# Extract and rank results

TweedSpot writes per-gene outputs into `rowData(input)`. The main result
columns are:

- `tweedspot_stat`: spatial smooth test statistic
- `tweedspot_pval`: raw p-value
- `tweedspot_padj`: adjusted p-value
- `tweedspot_edf`: effective degrees of freedom of the spatial smooth
- `tweedspot_dev_expl`: deviance explained by the fitted GAM

`get_tweedspot_results()` returns a clean `data.frame` representation of these
results. By default it sorts by adjusted p-value, breaking ties by
`tweedspot_stat`.

```{r inspect-results}
res <- get_tweedspot_results(spe_res)

head(res)
```

`top_spatial_genes()` provides a convenience wrapper for retrieving the top
hits by adjusted p-value, raw p-value, statistic, or deviance explained.

```{r top-genes}
top_spatial_genes(spe_res, n = 10, rank_by = "padj")
```

# Cell-type-specific spatial variation

With single-cell-resolution data, a feature can look spatially variable only
because cell types are arranged in space: a marker of one cell type is high
wherever that cell type sits. Setting `group` to a cell-type column tests each
feature *within* each cell type instead, so only spatial variation among cells
of the same type is called. Size factors and coordinates are shared across
types, each type gets its own spatial smooth, and p-values are adjusted
stage-wise: a feature is first screened across all types, then confirmed type
by type.

As a small real example we use Slide-seqV2 data from the mouse hippocampus
(Stickels et al., 2021), in which each bead carries a cell-type label from RCTD
(Cable et al., 2022). To keep the example fast we take the three most common
cell types, 1,500 beads of each, and the 25 most highly expressed genes.

```{r cell-type-data}
spe_hpc <- STexampleData::SlideSeqV2_mouseHPC()
spe_hpc <- spe_hpc[, !is.na(spe_hpc$celltype)]

top_types <- names(sort(table(spe_hpc$celltype), decreasing = TRUE))[1:3]
set.seed(1)
keep_beads <- unlist(lapply(top_types, function(ct) {
  idx <- which(spe_hpc$celltype == ct)
  idx[sample.int(length(idx), min(1500L, length(idx)))]
}))
spe_hpc <- spe_hpc[, sort(keep_beads)]

# Library-size factors from all genes, before keeping only a few of them.
lib <- MatrixGenerics::colSums(counts(spe_hpc))
spe_hpc$sizeFactor <- lib / mean(lib)

spe_hpc <- filter_features(
  spe_hpc,
  min_total = 50,
  exclude_mito = TRUE,
  group = "celltype",
  smooth_k = 20
)
top_genes <- order(MatrixGenerics::rowSums(counts(spe_hpc)), decreasing = TRUE)[1:25]
spe_hpc <- spe_hpc[top_genes, ]

table(spe_hpc$celltype)
```

We fit TweedSpot twice: once ignoring cell types, and once within each cell
type.

```{r cell-type-fit}
overall <- tweedspot(spe_hpc, smooth_k = 20, seed = 1, BPPARAM = bp,
                     verbose = FALSE)
by_type <- tweedspot(spe_hpc, group = "celltype", smooth_k = 20, seed = 1,
                     BPPARAM = bp, verbose = FALSE)
```

Ignoring cell types, many genes look spatially variable. Within cell types,
fewer remain: genes called only in the first analysis vary in space mainly
because the cell types they mark are arranged in space.

```{r cell-type-compare}
called_overall <- rowData(overall)$tweedspot_padj < 0.05
called_within <- rowData(by_type)$tweedspot_group_sig != ""
table(overall = called_overall, within_cell_type = called_within)

# Genes called overall but in no cell type: candidate composition effects
rownames(spe_hpc)[called_overall & !called_within]

# One row per gene and cell type
res_ct <- get_tweedspot_results(by_type, group = TRUE)
head(res_ct[, c("feature", "group", "n_detected", "padj", "dev_expl")])

# Top hits within the most common cell type
top_spatial_genes(by_type, n = 5, group = top_types[1])
```

`plot_feature()` and `plot_top_features()` take the same `group` argument and
show the model fitted on that cell type's beads only.

```{r cell-type-plot, fig.width=7.2, fig.height=2.9}
best <- top_spatial_genes(by_type, n = 1, group = top_types[1])$feature
plot_feature(by_type, best, group = top_types[1])
```

The same argument works with any discrete location label, such as cell states
or annotated regions.

# Visualize spatial patterns

`plot_feature()` shows one feature in three aligned panels: the observed
normalized signal, the TweedSpot fit on the same colour scale, and the fitted
spatial effect as a log2 fold change relative to the feature's average. It
refits the model with the settings `tweedspot()` stored in
`metadata(spe_res)$tweedspot`, so the figure shows exactly the model that was
tested.

```{r plot-feature, fig.width=7.2, fig.height=2.9}
top_feature <- rownames(res)[1]
plot_feature(spe_res, top_feature)
```

`plot_top_features()` draws the spatial effects of the `n_top` most
significant features on one shared scale, so the strength of different
patterns can be compared directly.

```{r plot-top, fig.width=7.2, fig.height=5}
plot_top_features(spe_res, n_top = 6)
```

Both functions save publication-ready files when given an `output_dir`, which
is created if needed. The default size, 7.2 inches wide, is a two-column journal
width.

```{r save-plots, eval=FALSE}
plot_feature(spe_res, top_feature, output_dir = "figures", formats = c("pdf", "png"))
plot_top_features(spe_res, n_top = 9, output_dir = "figures")
```

# Notes

- Covariates are specified from `colData(input)` using a one-sided formula such
  as `~ batch + age + sex`.
- If `colData(input)$sizeFactor` is present, TweedSpot uses it as the library
  size adjustment. Otherwise, `size_factor_method = "scran"` estimates size
  factors with `scran::computeSumFactors()`. Users can set
  `size_factor_method = "library_size"` for total-count scaling.
- `filter_features()` can optionally report how many features and locations
  were retained and how many were removed by each criterion.
- `tweedspot()` can print lightweight progress messages through
  `verbose = TRUE`.
